title: When the piggy bank is full: the satisfying next step
description: The pig will not take one more coin — which is not a problem but a graduation. Counting, rolling and banking a full piggy bank turns a pile of loose change into a number, a deposit and a new goal.

body.heading: Count it like a bank would
paragraphs: Empty the pig onto a table and sort before you count: coins into piles by denomination, notes flat and faced the same way. Count each pile twice — once stacking, once recording — because a full piggy bank routinely holds more than its owner guesses, and the true total is half the pleasure.

Roll or bag the coins if your bank asks for it, and keep a written tally as you go. This small ceremony matters: money that has been counted is money with a job, while money still sloshing in a pig is money that can quietly leak away on nothing.

body.heading: Bank it, name it, refill the pig
paragraphs: Deposit the total promptly — into the savings account or towards the goal the pig was feeding — and write the amount and date on a card kept with the pig. A named destination ('the deposit reached $212 on Saturday') is what separates a savings habit from a coin collection.

Then start the pig again the same day, with the next goal written on that same card. An empty piggy bank is not a sad sight; it is a tool reset. The fullest pig in the house is simply the one whose owner keeps graduating it.

takeaway: A full piggy bank is a graduation: sort and count the coins twice, deposit the total towards its named goal, record it — and restart the pig the same day.
